facts: Including programming at school as well as professionally, I started using AI for programming more than two years before the original interview.
For professional programming specifically, I started using AI about two years before the original interview.
I use GitHub Copilot for AI support at work; later in this interview I explain that our license is permanently configured in our editor.
I also use ChatGPT in the browser for AI support.
GitHub Copilot is my main AI tool, and recently at work we have also been using a tool called Open Code.
Open Code is free and open source; we connected our GitHub Copilot license to it so we can use the tool with the benefit of paid models. I compared it to something transcribed as 'cloud code'.
In the Open Code setup I described, the connected GitHub Copilot license provides access to the paid models as an engine.
Yep, yep, yeah, we can go there.
AI is integrated in the editors that we use or in Open Code, as far as I am describing our setup.
Our AI license is permanently configured in our editor, but we actually interact with AI only when we use the AI interface.
Actual interaction with AI happens when I interact with the AI interface in the editor.
Yeah, so yeah.
I mainly use AI for code analysis and to understand things I am unsure about, asking it questions or asking how something works, such as a built-in library method.
I ask AI about library methods or other things I want to understand; I may also ask an AI agent to implement a new feature I am working on.
I use AI often for writing and generating code.
I would say I sometimes use AI for debugging or fixing bugs.
I sometimes use AI for refactoring.
I rarely use AI to write tests because I typically write my own tests.
I use the tests I write myself as guardrails for the code generated by AI. I then moved on to the documentation category.
I rarely use AI for writing documentation.
I rarely use AI for documentation because my team does not really write documentation. I use AI very often for explaining concepts and learning.

On the Friday before the original interview, I worked on a pending ticket introducing a feature similar to a filter in our web application. I gave this as the task example requested in the no-AI workflow section.
The feature was an exception summary that lets users of our shipping company's web application see a count of containers meeting a condition, for example whether they have arrived.
The exception summary can show a count such as five containers that have arrived at their destination; clicking it filters the list to those five containers. I was working on extending that feature.

I was adding a new filter to the exception summary and we found a bug in one implementation. I read the code myself to understand what happens from the user's button click through the API request to the backend and what it triggers. I typically do not use AI for this reading because the way things work does not click in my head otherwise.

After reading the code and thinking I had found the issue, I wrote a learning test. In this case the relevant function converted a string representation of a number to an integer using a built-in library.
I had never used that built-in library before. For some reason it did not return an error when the string passed to it was not a number. I wrote a test to see how it behaved and found a problem.
The second step of my bug-fixing workflow was writing a learning test after reading the code.
After the learning test, I modified the existing production tests for the affected part of the code so that they failed by deliberately triggering the problem.

After deliberately making the production tests fail, I changed the production code, ran the tests and all passed. I pushed the fix and it went live in production. At this point in the interview I described the task as not involving AI; later I reported asking an AI agent about the bug.
I typically prefer to fix bugs myself, even if that is slower, because otherwise I do not develop my own understanding of how my product works.
In the general programming-activity frequency table, I rated writing code as very often; I later repeated that rating after clarifying the table.

I initially said bug fixing was often, then asked whether the table concerned AI versus non-AI or activities in general. After asking to restart, I rated writing code very often and reviewing code sometimes.
In my typical work in general, bug fixing and debugging are sometimes, while testing is very often.
I often work on specification and requirements in my typical working day.
In my typical working day, I write documentation almost never and learn often.
My team and I are extreme programming practitioners; one of the practices we follow daily is TDD, test-driven development.
TDD, one of the practices in our team's extreme programming approach, means test-driven development.

Whenever we fix or change code or add a new feature, we start with tests and try to create a whole test suite even for a function. In our team's TDD workflow, writing tests takes more time than writing the actual production code.
Ha, yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah, let me think about it for a second.
When first asked for another recent example of writing code or testing, I could not remember one immediately, so I checked our board.
And...Yeah, okay, okay, and I know what, and...What was the question again? So I just answered particularly to that.

About two weeks before the original interview we introduced a completely new feature to our system. Our application displays shipping containers; this is the recent example I gave for writing code and testing.

Users can click a container in our application to see its specific page and create a link for somebody who does not need authentication. Ordinarily, reaching the page requires being a user of our platform.
When we want to share container information with other people, we create what we call sharing links.

Anyone with a container sharing link can open it in a browser without logging in and see a container summary. Internal company employees also use these links very often, probably for customer requests, government matters, customs, or similar purposes.

Internal users requested a way to send an Excel file listing containers and get back a list of sharing-link URLs, rather than clicking each container separately. My manager asked me to implement that.

For the bulk sharing-links feature I started with tests, adding no production code until it was almost completely covered by tests. We then added production code incrementally once the tests were there.
Near the end of implementing the bulk sharing-links feature, I was confident it worked as expected, pushed it, and it was released to production.
Yep.
Yeah, I don't know if that answers the question. Okay.

I work with code I did not write all the time. My product is mature, has been out for seven years as of the original interview, and my team is the third wave of developers responsible for it, so most code was written by others.
At the original interview I had been in my team for almost two years. I estimate that I wrote probably 5–10% of the code base, perhaps closer to 5%; the rest was written by others or my colleagues.
Some of the code I did not write was written by my current colleagues.

I sometimes write tests for existing code, not just because it is working code, but when there is a bug or when I need to add a new feature on top of an existing feature; for example, I may write a learning test.
For existing production code I may add a characterization test, meaning a different test case, perhaps for something previously uncovered. I add the test without changing production code.
So, yeah.
And.Yeah.Yeah.
Yeah.
My team and I do not really feel that we have to use AI simply for its own sake.
We have been receiving encouragement or pressure from management or higher levels to use AI more.
Management or higher levels are pushing us to use more AI, but I think our team was already very productive and fast because of our particular ways of working.
We are not using AI because we need it; rather, we are trying to adapt our skill set to the AI tools available.
If future ways of working are all through AI tools, we want to know how to use those tools, so we are trying to develop that skill.

A few weeks before the original interview, when we had to extend the feature again, our team set an internal challenge to do it with AI and not write any code manually. We met together in a meeting room and more or less knew the code.
For the internal AI-only challenge, we knew the code to change from recent work and asked an AI agent to do all the work, giving it a prompt describing the outcome we wanted.

I think in the same prompt for the AI-only challenge we shared a JSON response or structured output showing what the API or feature should return. There was some back-and-forth with the agent, but it completed the task.
Yeah.
Yes, I have completed similar programming tasks without AI.
In the AI-only example I described, the result was exactly what we had hoped for; the process was the main difference from working without AI.
The AI-assisted feature-extension process was much faster: we completed it in two hours, and I estimated it would probably have taken two working days without AI.
By two working days I meant two full workdays of about 7.5–8 hours each. The drawback, in my team's view, was that we still needed to spend time reading the generated code afterwards.
Our industry is very data-intensive and we have big, important customers, so we cannot afford mistakes.
We focus heavily on quality and ended up reading the generated code anyway, but using AI was definitely faster for building and delivering that feature.
Completely, yeah.
Yeah.
Okay, so if I trust it, you mean...
When using AI for learning or discovery, I spar with the agent and ask questions such as how a function works.
For learning or sparring I typically trust AI answers 100% and do not really doubt them. In the bug example I described, I was unsure how a library worked.
While investigating the bug, I asked an AI agent to explain a code snippet, but was still unsure of its answer because I could see the function was triggering the bug.

To double-check the AI explanation of the library, I read its documentation, then wrote a learning test. For me that test is the absolute source of truth because I write it myself and see the outcome.
I write the test myself and observe the outcome. I would say I trust LLM answers on a 99% basis, but when an answer is code-related I do not really trust it.
I think AI is great for generating new code and similar things, but my company has many internal legacy systems, probably around 50 years old, with a great deal of internal logic and complexity.
AI can easily get confused by our company's complex legacy systems and internal logic.

I always double-check AI-generated code by running tests or rereading it. Sometimes after asking AI to generate code and running the tests, I flip or toggle values to see whether tests still pass or fail.
There's stuff like that, so yeah, yeah, I don't know if that answered the question, so yeah, yeah.
Yeah.
For AI-generated code I validate it, including by writing my own tests and checking it. For sparring and learning, I do not normally validate the AI's answers.
I normally do not validate AI answers when sparring or learning, unless the answer is extremely unusual.
In the year before the original interview, my team did not do any AI-related work.
Our team collaborates closely and pair-programs daily. The main reason we did not use much AI in the previous year was not lack of trust but psychological or safety concerns.
My colleagues were against AI in a way, possibly feeling threatened or thinking it was heavily hyped, so the team decided not to work with AI. Management requested that we start adding AI features.
The management requests I described were to add AI features just for the sake of it.

We did not add AI features simply for their own sake; we would add features to solve problems. At the beginning of the original interview year, we reevaluated and agreed to be more open to AI, not because trust had changed but to grow our skills and stay relevant to the market. There was also a change at the company level.
At the company level, the request evolved to using AI when it adds value for an internal or external user.
Regardless of position, people in my company are trying to develop their skills for working with AI. I found that development interesting in the year of the original interview.

entries.text: 强化学习与测试集应作概念区分：强化学习是通过环境反馈和奖励优化行动策略；测试集是在模型开发完成后估计泛化表现的数据。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。

数据泄漏与过拟合应作概念区分：数据泄漏是训练阶段不当使用了本应独立评估的信息；过拟合是模型学习了训练样本特有噪声而难以泛化。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
过拟合与大语言模型应作概念区分：过拟合是模型学习了训练样本特有噪声而难以泛化；大语言模型是从大规模文本等序列学习条件生成分布的模型。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
持续集成（continuous integration）：每次代码变更后自动执行构建与测试的流程。
代码审查与持续集成应作概念区分：代码审查是通过检查代码变更识别缺陷风险和可维护性问题；持续集成是每次代码变更后自动执行构建与测试的流程。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
精确率（precision）：预测为正的样本中实际为正的比例。
欠拟合与大语言模型应作概念区分：欠拟合是模型表达能力或训练程度不足导致规律学习不充分；大语言模型是从大规模文本等序列学习条件生成分布的模型。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
精确率与召回率应作概念区分：精确率是预测为正的样本中实际为正的比例；召回率是实际为正的样本中被正确识别的比例。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
模型幻觉（hallucination）：模型输出缺少可靠依据或包含错误断言的现象。
